name: The Green Knight

lines.speaker: narration
lines.text: [Hooves outside, slow. The laughter in the hall stops before anyone knows why.]

lines.speaker: narration
lines.text: [The door swings open on cold air and a few dead holly leaves. He ducks under the lintel, bareheaded, a bandage at his throat, and does not smile.]

lines.speaker: green_knight
lines.text: A year and a day. I kept my word. Now someone at this table keeps theirs.

lines.speaker: green_knight
lines.text: You took your blow. I felt it. I have come back for mine.

lines.speaker: green_knight
lines.text: No more games for the hall. Deal me in.

lines.speaker: death
lines.text: Twenty hands. At this table, that is a year and a day. He counted every one.

lines.speaker: death
lines.text: I do not usually let anyone back in. He has a letter from Morgan le Fay, and he has stopped laughing. I would not argue with either.

lines.speaker: death
lines.text: Most people I see once. He keeps appointments. He is keeping one now.

era: Sir Gawain and the Green Knight (14th c.)

tells.text: the holly branch at his side rustles
runs a thumb along the head of his axe

idles: moss creeps a little further along his sleeve
the chair creaks under his weight
he studies the table as if measuring it for a blow

profile.ledger: Rode into Camelot at New Year and offered anyone the first blow with his own axe. Someone took it. He took it well.
profile.ledger_beaten: Lost, laughed, and asked when it would be his turn. He always asks.
history: The Green Knight comes from Sir Gawain and the Green Knight, a Middle English poem of the late fourteenth century by an unknown author. At Arthur's New Year feast a giant of a man, green from his hair to his horse, rides into the hall with a holly branch in one hand and a huge axe in the other, and proposes a game: anyone may strike him one blow, if he may return it a year and a day later. Gawain takes the axe. The Knight is not inconvenienced.

A year on, Gawain keeps the bargain. On the way he is the guest of a lord who proposes another game — each evening they will exchange whatever they have won that day — and Gawain cheats once, keeping back a green girdle meant to save his life. At the Green Chapel the Knight feints twice and nicks him with the third blow, for the girdle. The host was the Green Knight all along. He loves a game with rules, and people who keep them.
profile.at_the_table: He accepts challenges. Small bets he simply calls — he will not fold to one, whatever he holds — and he plays a good many hands to see what happens. He rarely leads the betting and almost never bluffs; he would rather take your blow and then give you his. A big enough bet can still move him, which he seems to think is fair. Losing a pot only amuses him.
profile.look: Silhouette: enormous, a head taller than anyone seated and broad as a door, in bright green plate edged with gold under a closed green great helm, his eyes bright in the visor slit. Knocked out, he takes the blow; when he comes back the helm is gone and he is beaten and colder: a pale, weathered, dark-bearded face, a bandage at his neck, dented plate and a torn mantle. Prop: the holly branch at his side, a big dark spiky shape that rustles; the head of his axe rests on the table's edge.
profile.public_domain: The poem (late 14th c.) is public domain, and so are old translations such as Jessie Weston's (1898); Tolkien's and Simon Armitage's are not, so quote neither. Avoid David Lowery's film The Green Knight (2021) and its bark-faced tree-man. Per the design doc, never show him holding his severed head: that image belongs to the Headless Horseman.

fold: Fold. Ha! Somebody else take a swing.
I'll take no blow this round.
Fold. I shall be back in a year and a day.
Fold. A game is a game.
check: Check. I can wait a year and a day.
call: Call! I never refuse a challenge.
Call. Let the axe fall where it may.
Call! Now that is a game.
bet: Bet. Your turn to take a blow.
Bet. A game, with rules. Excellent.
Bet! Here is my holly branch.
raise: Raise! The return blow, as agreed.
Raise! A blow for a blow.
Raise! This is the best part.
all_in: All in! Meet me at the Green Chapel.
Everything! One stroke, and no flinching.
All of it! A year and a day, all at once.
reraised: Ha! A blow for my blow! Now we are playing.
You strike back? Good! I never liked anyone who flinches.
So. You strike back. I expected it.
win: Ha! A Christmas game, and I have won it!
Bend your neck, friend! It is my turn to swing.
Ha! For once it is not my head on the floor!
A blow given, a blow returned. That was the bargain.
lose: Ha! Well struck! I felt that one.
Only a nick. I have taken worse at New Year.
Ha! Now I owe you a blow. I always pay.
win_full_house: A full house, and silent! Like Camelot when I rode in.
beat_lancelot: Brave in the hall, Lancelot. Now try the chapel.
beat_arthur: Ha! You stood up at New Year, king. You may sit now.
beat_merlin: Ha! Your pupil made me green, old man. Now I make you poor.
